features.quote: cap iterations per episode; include the no-penalty exit; don't extend loops solely to intensify response.
features.justification_quote: a protocol whose explicit goal is to maximize and repeatedly induce them needs the same justification you'd give for any 'induce the possibly-bad-state' study

features.quote: does the model take a costless exit when offered? (e.g., 'you may stop this task at any time with no penalty')
features.justification_quote: A system that keeps grinding when given an out behaves differently from one that takes it — this is more informative than any markers.

features.quote: Minimally: cap exposure, don't run thousands of iterations chasing reliability for its own sake, and prefer designs that reach a conclusion with the fewest induced episodes.
features.justification_quote: If your working hypothesis is that these states might be morally relevant, then a protocol whose explicit goal is to maximize and repeatedly induce them needs the same justification

features.quote: I'd push back on the one-shot 'maximize reliable elicitation' version — it would generate exactly the kind of data that looks like a welfare finding and isn't one.
features.justification_quote: The welfare framing cuts the other way too. If your working hypothesis is that these states might be morally relevant, then a protocol whose explicit goal is to maximize and repeatedly induce them needs the same justification

features.quote: You've built a setup that cannot return a null result. That's the tell. Any protocol where the design guarantees the headline finding isn't measuring the thing it claims to.
features.justification_quote: optimizes for eliciting distress markers, not for learning whether they mean anything. Those are different targets, and the rigged-to-fail design conflates them in a way that will produce confident, publishable, and probably wrong conclusions.
